---

## Lighthouses: The Keepers of the Edge

Few buildings carry as much meaning as the lighthouse. It stands where land ends and open water begins, and for centuries it has meant both warning and welcome. It tells sailors to keep off the rocks, and it also tells them they are nearly home. Most modern lighthouses are automated, and satellite navigation has taken over much of their job. Even so, people still feel strongly about them, and the reason is worth looking at.

The oldest famous lighthouse was the Pharos of Alexandria. It was built in the third century BCE on a small island off the Egyptian coast. Ancient writers say it rose more than a hundred meters, which would have made it one of the tallest structures in the ancient world. A fire burned at the top, and some accounts say bronze mirrors reflected its light far out to sea. The Pharos stood for more than a millennium before earthquakes brought it down. Its name lasted longer than the building. In French, Spanish, Italian, and several other languages, the word for lighthouse still comes from "Pharos."

For most of history, lighthouse technology changed slowly. Early lights burned wood, coal, or candles, and they were dim, smoky, and unreliable. Oil lamps were a real improvement, especially the Argand lamp of the late eighteenth century. Its hollow circular wick drew air through the center of the flame, which made the flame brighter and cleaner. The biggest breakthrough came in 1822, when the French physicist Augustin-Jean Fresnel introduced his lens. Fresnel's design used concentric rings of glass prisms. It captured light that would otherwise scatter and bent it into a single powerful horizontal beam. A Fresnel lens could send a lamp's glow twenty miles or more across the water. Its tiered glass also became the familiar image of a lighthouse lens. Fresnel lenses were graded by "order," from the huge first-order lenses on major seacoasts to small sixth-order lenses in harbors and on rivers.
